title: SLO Regression: KV-cache repopulation and batching contention postmortem
body:
Summary:

On 2024-11-13 at ~14:05 UTC we observed a progressive SLO regression for tail-latency on the hosted inference tier for text-generation routes using gptx-8k variants. The reported symptom from customer and internal SLO dashboards: 99th percentile p95/p99 token latency rose from baseline ~180ms to peaks ~1.2s across a subset of pods. The issue lasted in measurable form until the hotfix rollout completed at 17:35 UTC.

Impact:
- Affected customers: ~18 active tenants (medium+ allocations) running conversational workloads; estimated 3% of total hosted traffic during the window.
- Observable metric regressions: p95 token latency +2–6x, request CPU steal and context-switch rates increased, GPU utilization decreased on impacted hosts (indicative of CPU-side stalls).
- Customer-facing: elevated error/timeout retries for long-conversation workloads; one customer escalated for SLA breach and wanted detailed validation steps.

How we detected it:
- Alerting: anomaly on the per-route 99th latency alerted at 14:12 UTC (automated SLO monitor).
- Pager: on-call, Miguel (serving-runtime), paged at 14:14 UTC.
- Initial triage pointed at increased host-level CPU time and higher number of KV-cache misses for long prefix requests.

Immediate mitigation timeline (high-level):
- 14:18 UTC: Throttled non-critical background cache warming jobs and disabled scheduled global cache warm for that cluster.
- 14:35 UTC: Scoped traffic routing to fallback model variant (gptx-8k-quant-2) for the most affected shard set as emergency mitigation.
- 15:10 UTC: Roll forward a targeted hotfix (PR 1587) that gated concurrent cache repopulation under a single-writer lock and reduced default batch window for the problematic route. Started canary on 4 pods.
- 16:25 UTC: Canary showed p99 latency improvement ~60% vs impacted pods and stable CPU profiles.
- 17:35 UTC: Hotfix fully rolled out to all pods in the affected pool.

Root cause analysis (detailed):
- Primary root cause: A regression in the cache invalidation path introduced during the September optimization for aggressive KV caching. The optimization created a race where, under certain long-sequence request patterns, multiple workers concurrently attempted to repopulate the KV prefix cache for the same model partition.

- Contributing factors:
  - Batching window reduction for low-latency customers (recent config change) increased the frequency of small batches touching the same prefixes, amplifying repopulation events.
  - The repopulation routine used optimistic per-shard population without a strong single-writer guard; on contended prefixes, this produced repeated reads/writes to shared in-memory structures causing lock contention and elevated context switches.
  - Lock contention manifested primarily on CPU (Python runtime threads) while GPUs stayed underutilized; inference kernels were waiting on KV state to be published.
  - A metric gap: we lacked a per-prefix repopulation counter and per-worker lock-wait histogram, making early detection of this exact pattern difficult.

Evidence gathered:
- CPU flamegraphs from two affected hosts (14:00–14:30 UTC) show repeated time spent in "kv_cache.repoppulate()" and "_acquire_shard_lock()" with many short-lived threads in waiting state.
- Tracing spans captured via our tracing hooks show repopulation spans (avg 35–120ms) occurring concurrently for identical prefix keys.
- Histograms: per-route batching size distribution shifted left post-config change, with spikes in 1–3 token batches.
- GPU telemetry: low active SM utilization during the incident window while CPU sys/cpu-wait rose ~30%.

Why the previous safeguards didn't stop it:
- We had a heuristic to avoid duplicate repopulation if a "recently repopulated" flag existed, but it assumed monotonic increases in prefix traffic; unusual conversational patterns with simultaneous near-zero window requests bypassed the heuristic.
- The September change removed a locking guard to reduce latency under typical loads; that optimization assumed negligible contention which proved false for these workloads.

Hotfix details and validation plan:
- Hotfix (PR 1587) summary: Introduced a single-writer gate per prefix key implemented with a fast, low-contention in-memory lease (10s TTL) plus a fallback non-blocking enqueue for other workers. Also reduced the batch-aggregation window from 10ms to 6ms only for the impacted route group and added jitter to scheduled cache warmups to avoid thundering herd at minute boundaries.

Validation performed:
- Canary: 4 pods in a canary pool handled production traffic for 45 minutes under live load (16:25–17:10 UTC). During canary we observed:
  - p99 token latency returned to baseline within ~2 minutes of traffic steering.
  - Per-prefix repopulation rate dropped ~90% on canary pods.
  - CPU sys/wait normalized and GPU utilization increased toward normal operating ratios.
- Synthetic load tests: Replayed captured request traces with extreme conversational concurrency (captured 2k multi-turn sequences) against a staging cluster with and without the hotfix. Results: hotfix reduced repopulation CPU overhead by median 78% and p99 token latency improved from 1.1s to 0.19s.
- Regression checks: Verified there was no measurable increase in cold-start latencies or tail latencies for unrelated routes.

Post-incident monitoring and follow-ups (action items):
1) Instrumentation
   - Add per-prefix repopulation counters and per-worker lock-wait histograms (owner: Lina Zhao, due: 2024-11-30).
   - Add an anomaly detector rule for rapid increase in repopulation events per-prefix (owner: Ben Carter, due: 2024-12-05).
2) Code/Runtime
   - Keep single-writer lease mechanism but iterate on lease TTL heuristics; evaluate whether lease-based approach can be generalized (owner: Aisha Patel, PR follow-ups in 1589, due: 2024-12-12).
   - Re-run static analysis for other optimistic-population paths introduced in September change; create tickets for hardening (owner: Miguel Torres, due: 2024-11-22).
3) Configuration and SLOs
   - Revert aggressive batch-window shrink for low-latency profile until we can A/B test safely across more traffic (owner: Product-hosted-api, liaison: Priya Menon, due: 2024-11-21).
   - Update runbooks: include steps to detect per-prefix repopulation storms and emergency throttles for background warmups (owner: eng-sre, due: 2024-11-25).
4) Customer remediation
   - For the customer who escalated (acct: AcroMed), provide a short write-up of root cause, timelines, and validation artifacts; offer a technical review call (owner: Customer Success; support ticket JIRA-CS-2219, due: 2024-11-18).

Known risks and TODOs:
- Lease approach can mask slow repopulation if the writer fails mid-population; need a stronger liveness probe and fallback enqueue logic to ensure eventual consistency (todo: design review 2024-11-20).
- We still need to verify long-tail conversation patterns across other model families (gptx-16k variants) — scheduled load replay next week (owner: Miguel Torres).

Appendix: quick notes from profiling session (raw bullet points)
- Host i-0abc: repetitive stack: kv_cache.repopulate -> lock_acquire -> pyobject_wait -> epoll_wait.
- Trace IDs: 20241113-TL-001 .. TL-008 show identical prefix key collisions.
- PR 1587 introduced: prefix-lease.py, cache-warm-jitter, batch-window-config paramization.

Conclusions:
The incident was the result of a correctness/performance regression in a cache repopulation optimization combined with a configuration change that increased small-batch frequency. The immediate hotfix effectively mitigated the observed SLO regressions and returned tail latencies to baseline. The long-term plan is to add better telemetry to detect this pattern earlier, harden optimistic population paths, and be more conservative with micro-optimizations that remove locking without strong observational evidence across diverse traffic shapes.

If you have additional logs/trace samples to attach, paste links into the linked_artifacts section or ping #serving-runtime-incidents on Slack.

Prepared by: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
Reviewed by: Miguel Torres, Lina Zhao
